source_read: PMC full text PMC5341491 (publisher version, Psychological Medicine 47(5):971-980, open access; not an author manuscript), all sections, Tables 1-3, read in the built-in browser in my own tab on 2026-10-27; online supplement (Tables S1-S2, Figs S1-S3) not read

claims.overstatement: None for the figures attributed to this source: each matches the source with the right unit (per doubling of the odds of ever use), the right exposure (genetic liability to ever use, ICC ever/never phenotype) and the right outcome (schizophrenia case status, PGC2). Two omissions, not overstatements: (1) the claim does not say that none of the 21 variants reached genome-wide significance (all at p < 10^-5; the authors say some may be false positives); (2) the authors' own reading (some evidence of a small causal effect of initiation; at most a 24% higher relative risk at the upper confidence bound for 50% vs 10% probability of initiation; stronger evidence for the reverse direction) is not given, although the claim gives the narrative reviews' readings. 'Pleiotropy-robust' for MR-Egger is acceptable; the source calls it 'more robust to pleiotropy' (valid under its own assumption).
claims.note: Gage's 'where this is reported' instrument strength: the paper gives no F statistic and no variance explained by the 21 SNPs; the 13-20% in the Method is the SNP-based variance explained by the whole-genome GWAS of ever use, not the instrument, and must not be used as instrument strength. Sensitivity analyses for other pathways: MR-Egger (intercept OR 0.99, 0.98-1.01, p = 0.50), 12-SNP restriction, leave-one-out (supplement only), positive control education (weak, 0.99, 0.97-1.00, p = 0.066) and negative control height (null, 1.00, 0.99-1.01). Reverse-direction MR-Egger 1.17 (0.96-1.43), p = 0.13, is not in the claim and is the one figure that weakens the reverse-direction result the claim cites. Units: 1.04 per doubling corresponds to about 1.06 per unit of log odds (editors' conversion check: exp(ln 1.04 / 0.693) = 1.058), close to Vaucher's 1.08 per unit; the claim keeps the units apart correctly, but a reader comparing 1.04 with 1.08 may think the second is twice as large. Recomputed the authors' 24% upper bound: exp((logit 0.5 - logit 0.1) x ln(1.07)/0.693) = 1.239, same; the formula as printed in Method > Sensitivity analyses, 5th paragraph (log(UCB/0.693)) would give 2.60, so the printed formula has a misplaced bracket. 'These three studies share consortium data': for this source, exposure data are the ICC GWAS (Stringer et al. 2016) and outcome data PGC2 (2014), with an EGCUT overlap of about 1,500 people between the two; supported.

anchors.locator: Results > Effect of cannabis initiation on schizophrenia risk, 1st paragraph; Table 2, row 1
anchors.extracted: Inverse-variance-weighted two-sample MR (correlated likelihood method), 21 SNPs associated with ever/never cannabis use at p < 10^-5: OR for schizophrenia 1.04 (95% CI 1.01-1.07) per doubling of the odds of cannabis initiation, p = 0.019; outcome data 36,989 schizophrenia cases and 113,075 controls (PGC2).

anchors.locator: Results > Sensitivity analyses, 1st paragraph; Table 3, rows 1-2 (cannabis initiation -> schizophrenia, 21 SNPs)
anchors.extracted: MR-Egger with all 21 SNPs: intercept OR 0.99 (95% CI 0.98-1.01), p = 0.50 (little evidence of directional pleiotropy); causal estimate OR 1.01 (0.93-1.10), p = 0.815, weaker evidence with wider interval, described as not inconsistent with the main analysis.

anchors.locator: Results > Sensitivity analyses, 4th paragraph; Table 2, row 4; Table 3, rows 7-8
anchors.extracted: Restricted to the 12 SNPs available for the control analyses: OR 1.03 (95% CI 0.99-1.08), p = 0.145 in Table 2 (0.15 in the text); MR-Egger with these 12: intercept 1.00 (0.97-1.03), p = 0.801; causal 1.01 (0.88-1.17), p = 0.854.

anchors.locator: Results > Effect of schizophrenia risk on cannabis initiation, 1st paragraph; Table 2, row 5; Method (no subheading), 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Reverse direction: 107 of 128 genome-wide significant schizophrenia SNPs (the 128 explain about 18% of variance in schizophrenia risk) found in the ICC GWAS; OR for cannabis initiation 1.10 (95% CI 1.05-1.14) per doubling of the odds of schizophrenia, p = 2.64 x 10^-5; ICC sample 14,388 people who had ever used cannabis and 17,942 who had not.

anchors.locator: Results > Sensitivity analyses, 2nd paragraph; Table 3, last two rows
anchors.extracted: Reverse direction by MR-Egger: intercept OR 1.00 (0.98-1.01), p = 0.52; causal estimate 1.17 (0.96-1.43), p = 0.13 (0.128 in the table): larger point estimate, weaker evidence, interval includes 1.

Instrument: ICC GWAS of ever/never cannabis use (Stringer et al. 2016); no SNP reached genome-wide significance; 153 SNPs at p < 10^-5, pruned at r2 > 0.9 to 22, one removed for quality, 21 used (remaining correlations modelled). The whole-genome GWAS explained 13-20% of observed variation in ever use (SNP-based, not the instrument); no F statistic or variance explained by the 21 SNPs is reported in the main text.

anchors.locator: Method > Effect of cannabis initiation on schizophrenia risk, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Estimates per unit increase in the log odds of initiation were converted to the OR per doubling of the odds of the binary exposure (log OR x 0.693, then exponentiated), because the per-unit scale is hard to interpret.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Strengths and limitations, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: The ICC phenotype was a single question on ever use, so trying once and daily use for years are not distinguished; exposure intensity is the more likely risk factor; the variants may index impulsivity or risk taking rather than cannabis initiation itself. Results are not comparable to observational studies of heavier use or different strains; no variants index the strength (THC:CBD ratio) of cannabis used.

None of the instrument SNPs reached genome-wide significance; some may be false positives; authors expect the estimates to be overly conservative, and false-positive variants reduce power and could introduce pleiotropic variants.

anchors.locator: Discussion > Strengths and limitations, 2nd paragraph; Method (no subheading), 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Data sources: ICC (exposure) and PGC2 schizophrenia GWAS (outcome), plus SSGAC education and GIANT height for controls. The ICC and PGC2 overlap through the Estonian EGCUT cohort (2.3% of PGC2, about 10% of ICC; about 1,500 people); main analyses rerun without EGCUT in PGC2 gave unchanged results.

anchors.locator: Results > Sensitivity analyses, 6th paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Method > Sensitivity analyses, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Using the upper 95% bound (1.07), a person with a 50% probability of initiation has at most a 24% higher relative risk of schizophrenia than one with a 10% probability (recomputed: 1.239). Authors read the effect of initiation, if any, as likely small.

anchors.locator: Results > Positive and negative controls, 1st paragraph; Table 2, rows 2-3
anchors.extracted: Positive control (years in education, 126,599 people, 12 SNPs): 0.99 (0.97-1.00), p = 0.066, weaker than predicted; negative control (height, 253,288 people): 1.00 (0.99-1.01), p = 0.90, as predicted.

Authors' reading: some evidence that cannabis initiation increases schizophrenia risk, with a small causal estimate; stronger evidence that schizophrenia risk predicts initiation; the weak instrument limits interpretation; future schizophrenia GWAS should record cumulative cannabis exposure.

key_findings.note: Table 1 ranges check: beta for ever use 0.09 to 0.29 (SE 0.02 to 0.06), for schizophrenia -0.03 to 0.05; 13-20% is whole-genome, second-hand, as the card says.

Finding confirmed. The note's comparison figure (3.38% of liability variance in Pasman et al., 2018) comes from another source and was not checked here; the caution against quoting the 18% as instrument strength is right.
Paragraph numbers right (running text only; Table 3 sits between the 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
Recomputed: 1.239 with the intended formula, 2.60 with the formula as printed; point-estimate version 1.132.

reporting_issues.note: Method > Positive and negative controls says the linear coefficients were multiplied by 0.693 'for consistency'.
13 variants carry footnote a, 4 have proxies: 8 + 4 = 12; the text's 9 in the height study cannot be reconciled.
126,599 in Results; 126,559 in the reference title.

risk_of_bias.note: High overall for the forward estimate is defensible: the exclusion restriction is untested (the authors themselves name impulsivity and risk taking), MR-Egger is null and imprecise, and the positive control failed. The claim cites the reverse estimate too, for which the card's own judgment is some concerns; the claim's reasoning should carry that split. Editors' F >= about 20 per variant from p < 10^-5 recomputed (chi-square 19.51).

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The authors' wording is hedged ('some evidence', 'small'); the main stretch is calling the reverse result strong evidence for the reverse-causation hypothesis, which the card lists as gap (3).

missed: Discussion > Strengths and limitations, 5th paragraph: the reverse analysis assumes that schizophrenia variants act on behaviour in the general population, most of whom never develop schizophrenia (authors cite the psychosis continuum and childhood psychopathology findings). This bears directly on the claim's reading that genetic liability to schizophrenia makes cannabis use more likely.

Discussion > Strengths and limitations, 7th paragraph: MR-Egger tests biological (horizontal) pleiotropy only, not mediated pleiotropy, and the authors note that a genetic correlation (Verweij et al.) fits shared genetic architecture or causation in either direction; relevant to the claim's 'shared genetic liability' alternative.
